subject: treasureHoard
pitch:
Category: Prop group.
Subject: treasure hoard: coins, gems, chest, crown, goblets.
Style: League of Legends.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module for a League of Legends-style treasure hoard scene—chest, coins, gems, crown, goblets—using plain objects without joints since these are props rather than rigged characters.

I'm sticking to SDK APIs I'm confident about (builder primitives like joint, part, stick, sweep, lathe, extrude, loft, along, ring, paint, metal) plus the clockwork and glow kits, aiming for a substantial but manageable module with the chest sitting atop a coin pile base at ground level.

I'm planning the hoard as a single root joint with parts clustered around it: a dome-shaped mound built from a lathed profile, scattered with a few hundred small cylinder coins to suggest a pile without blowing the triangle budget, all finished in gilt metal. The chest itself will be a wooden box with iron bands and a rounded lid, likely built from a swept or lathed section to get the curved top.

Working out rotation math...

The CylinderGeometry with openEnded false gives half-disc caps, which works fine as a plain geometry placed directly rather than built via sweeps. Since props and scenery can be plain objects without joints, I'll keep this simple, but each geometry still needs to go through b.part to join the model via the builder.

I'm noting b.part's full signature with placement options like at, bone, frame, rotation in XYZ degrees, scale, and texture, and I'll rely on rotation for simplicity since I can't test the output directly. Now I'm sketching the overall scene layout in meters: a hoard footprint around 1.1m wide, with the chest centered at the back facing +Z toward the viewer, and a coin mound spilling forward with goblets and a crown placed on top.

I'm working out the coin mound as a lathe shape with a specific outline profile to create a rounded pile, planning to paint it with gold coloring.

I'm scattering coin geometry across the mound's surface using a seeded random function, embedding small cylindrical coins with randomized spin and filtering by surface normal so they sit naturally on the upper slopes, and varying their colors between gilt and metal tones for realism.

For the overall look, I'm leaning toward a stylized, LoL-inspired aesthetic with saturated gold, strong rim lighting, and glowing gems rather than photorealism, possibly using the clockwork metal kit combined with panel shading and gem glow effects to get that painterly, bold-color treasure pile feel.

I'm defining faceted gem shapes using lathe geometry with six-sided bipyramid outlines, assigning flat saturated colors for ruby, emerald, sapphire, and amethyst, and applying a glow effect since glow needs a material rather than a paint. For the chest itself, I'm planning a wooden box body with grain-textured paint, iron band reinforcements, a half-cylinder lid, a gilded lock plate with an embedded gem, and ornate gold trim, working out placement and dimensions for the chest body.

Now I'm calculating the lid geometry: a half-cylinder with radius matching half the chest depth, oriented along the X-axis and positioned so its flat face sits on top of the box body, making sure the rotation and axis alignment produce a proper arched lid shape.

For the iron bands across the lid, I'm planning to use thin half-cylinder shells at a few positions along the arch (like at x = -0.3, 0, 0.3), open-ended so they sit as decorative straps over the curved surface rather than solid caps.

Actually, I'm reconsidering and going simpler: rendering the bands as flat boxes mounted on the front face and lid, rather than curved shells. I'm working out the chest's orientation—front faces +Z, with the body spanning roughly z=-0.43 to 0.03—so vertical straps can be placed as thin boxes near the front face at the right x positions. Then I'm adding a lock plate as a small rotated cylinder centered on the front, possibly with a gem accent for a decorative touch.

Now I'm placing iron corner brackets as boxes along the four vertical body edges, considering gilding them for contrast, and defining a wood grain paint function for the body that creates plank seams with periodic darkening along the y-axis to simulate board gaps, plus deciding whether to apply the same paint to the lid top.

For the base, I'm skipping chest feet and instead thinking about how the coin mound interacts with the chest — since the chest body sits at y 0 to 0.36, placing the mound directly underneath would bury the front, so I'm shifting the mound center forward so it piles against the chest's front face and spills around it, accepting that the chest will intersect the mound slightly at the back since that part stays hidden.

To stop coins near the chest from clipping through its geometry, I'm filtering the scattered hits by position, keeping only ones whose z coordinate places them in front of the chest (or off to the sides), so the visible pile reads as heaped against and around the chest rather than poking through it. I'm also toying with the idea of showing the chest lid open with gold and gems spilling out for more visual impact, but that adds pivot/rotation complexity, so I might just keep the lid closed for simplicity.

Actually, I'm reconsidering a partially-open lid as a half-cylinder rotated roughly 40° about its back hinge edge, which means I need to recompute the lid's pivot position—since the lid's own rotation origin sits forward of the hinge, I have to offset it so that rotating about the hinge produces a correct opening motion rather than rotating in place.

Working through the lid's rotated position, I get the new axis point at [0, 0.492, -0.242]. Then for the chest interior, since the body is a closed box geometry, the top face would hide any treasure placed inside it, so I'm thinking the gold heap needs to sit above the box's top rim instead, visible through the gap left by the raised lid.

Checking the geometry though, the heap's height would collide with the open lid's arc near the hinge axis, so this spilling-treasure-with-open-lid approach gets complicated fast. Simpler to just keep the lid closed and pile the gold around the exterior of the chest instead, which reads fine visually without the overlap issues.

Now I'm sketching a crown to sit on top of the mound — a cylindrical band shell with conical spikes positioned around the rim and small gem accents, working out the lathe outline so the ring profile forms a proper closed loop without touching the axis.

I'm figuring out placement: positioning five cone points radially around the band using sine/cosine angles, then calculating where on the mound's sloped surface the crown should rest so its base sits naturally on the coin pile rather than floating above it.

Now I'm sketching the goblet's lathe profile—working out the radius-and-height coordinates for the foot, stem, and bowl, including a hollow inner wall so the bowl can later hold coins instead of being a solid shape.

I'm weighing whether to apply corner smoothing: with such a thin rim at the mouth, cutting the corners might cause the edges to self-intersect, so I'll skip smoothing and just add more points for a blockier, lowpoly look that still fits the stylized aesthetic.

For the goblets, I'm planning a gilt finish with cel-shaded highlights and possibly a cabochon gem stuck to the stem or foot via a surface attachment. I'm figuring out placement on the coin mound — working out the mound's radial height profile from its lathe outline so I can position each goblet's base at the correct height for its distance from center, sinking the foot slightly into the surface for a natural resting look.

Now I'm considering the chest's position at the back of the mound: at that location the mound rises enough that the chest's lower portion would be buried in coins, which actually reads nicely as the chest half-sunk into the treasure pile, with only its upper front face and lid visible above the gold.

Thinking about alternatives, I wonder if it's better to elevate the chest atop a flattened plateau on the mound's crest rather than burying it, so the whole hoard still reads as resting on the ground while the chest sits visibly on top of the coin pile.

Checking corner distances against the mound profile, there's a risk of the chest's back corners floating above the mound surface by a noticeable gap, which would look off unless coins are scattered densely enough to visually mask it.

I'm leaning toward a simpler setup: place the chest directly on the floor and let a separate coin mound spread in front and around it, carefully filtering the coin scatter so it never overlaps the chest geometry, then checking the footprint corners against the mound's radius to confirm nothing floats awkwardly.

Let me settle on a smaller mound, around 0.2 height, with the chest's lower front embedded in it, and add scattered coins lying flat on the floor in an annulus outside the mound radius to extend the treasure spill without cluttering under the chest.

I'm scaling the whole hoard down for realism, setting the mound radius near 0.5-0.6, chest width around 0.64 with a 0.3-tall body and a 0.2-radius lid giving a top height of 0.5, and placing the chest front flush at z=0 while checking how the mound profile height interacts with the chest's front corners.

Testing different mound center positions, I keep finding the chest gets buried too deep -- if I set the mound peak near the chest center, the body ends up half-submerged, which looks wrong. The better approach is to treat the chest as sitting on top of the pile rather than embedded within it, so I'm reworking the placement to rest the chest's base at the mound's surface height rather than intersecting it.

So the mound gets a flat plateau of radius 0.42 at height 0.12, sloping down to zero at radius 0.7, with the chest sitting centered on top and the corner distance of 0.37 fitting safely within the plateau. I'll filter out coin scatter points that fall under the chest footprint so they don't poke through, keeping coins visible around the sides of the chest on the plateau and down the mound's slope — giving that classic look of a treasure chest resting atop a pile of coins.

I'm defining the mound's lathe profile as a series of radius/height points from base to plateau to center, closing the outline so it revolves into a solid shape, and checking that the chest's footprint sits comfortably inside the flat top. For the mound's material, I'm leaning toward a brass or gilt metal finish with some tarnish and polish variation, since the coins scattered on top will provide most of the visual texture anyway.

I'm planning roughly 150 small cylindrical coins on the mound plus 40 on the floor, each a tiny stick part with a flat gold, silver, or bronze color cycled across a handful of shades, keeping the total triangle count well within budget. I'm also weighing whether to stamp coin faces with a texture, but worrying that applying a texture to a cylinder would also wrap unwanted detail onto the sides, so flat colors might be the simpler and safer choice.

I'm deciding to use textured coin faces anyway for a handful of coins, designing a gold circular emblem (crown, star, sun variants) that maps cleanly onto the top cap since the coin's orientation faces outward, while the hidden bottom cap doesn't matter — and since colored drawings override the part's color property, I can assign these without conflicting with the coin's base color.

I'm budgeting the texture atlas to stay within 4-5 distinct images: two coin faces, and a decorative emblem plate for the chest lock area (a shield sigil texture on a plane in front of the lock) to make the chest read better, skipping extras like sparkle cards on the floor. For gems, I'm planning to use lathe-shaped six-sided gems with glowing emissive colors, placed around the lock, in the crown, on goblets, and scattered across the treasure mound.

I'm working through where exactly to place the crown relative to the mound and chest, checking whether various spots fall on the plateau or the slope so it doesn't float or look awkwardly tilted. Given the crown's size relative to the chest's footprint, I'm leaning toward resting it on the coin pile in front of the chest rather than off to the side on the slope.

Since a lathe mound is axially symmetric, I'm considering adding a smaller secondary lathe-generated pile in front of the chest, unioned with the main one, to give a natural perch for the crown and goblets near the chest's front edge — checking that its intersection with the chest stays hidden in the coins. I'm sketching the outline points for this front pile so its top sits at roughly the right height for the crown to rest flush.

Now I'm working out goblet placements on the front pile's slope, computing the pile's local height at various radii from its center so the goblets sit naturally embedded rather than floating, and checking whether they'd fall off the pile's edge onto the floor or onto the main mound's slope instead.

Checking goblet feet contact and chest placement on the plateau both line up fine. For gems and coins, I plan to scatter them across the mound and front pile surfaces using filtered surface hits—favoring upward-facing points and avoiding the floor—then stick each piece with slight embedding and random spin, though I need to make sure the chest geometry is built before the surface query so coins don't accidentally land inside it.

I realize I should exclude any hits that fall within the chest's footprint on the plateau, since those would end up buried and poking through rather than visible. The scatter function supports filter and keepOut parameters, so I can just check hit positions against the chest's x/z bounds to skip them.

Now I'm working out coin placement details: minDist spacing to avoid overcrowding, using a small embed fraction so coins sit half-buried into the surface, and letting them inherit surface normals so stacked coins tilt naturally on slopes. For the floor ring, I'm placing coins in an annulus outside the mound radius with slight random tilts (kept under 10°) so they lie mostly flat without visibly sinking into the ground, checking that the tilt-induced dip stays well within acceptable tolerance relative to the model's overall height.

I realize the annulus needs to be centered on point M (not the origin, since M sits at z=-0.2) and should also avoid overlapping the front pile P, so I'm adjusting the radius range and considering filtering out coins too close to P's base. I'm also thinking about scattering a few glowing gems across the floor surfaces for visual interest.

Now I'm designing the chest geometry: setting body height to 0.26 and base offset Y0=0.12, giving a body top around 0.38 and lid arc peaking near 0.58, for a total chest height of about 0.6 meters to match realistic proportions.

Working out the lid's half-cylinder construction, rotated so its arc faces upward and its flat base meets the body top, matching the body's width and length exactly.

Then I'm adding the thin iron band shells with openEnded true, positioned along the lid at a slightly larger radius so they wrap over the lid's surface near its ends and center, with open flat edges that stay hidden since the lid and body cover them.

Next I'm placing vertical iron straps as thin boxes on the chest's front face at the center and both sides, slightly protruding outward, plus corner brackets as boxes near the chest's edges top and bottom to simulate reinforcement. Then I start on the lock plate, positioning a small gilt cylinder rotated to face outward on the front of the chest.

For the lock's emblem, I'm layering a textured plane with an SVG crest (shield and crown) just in front of the gilt plate, and considering adding a separate glowing gem sphere embedded in the emblem's center for extra detail.

Now I'm working out the chest's side handles — small torus rings rotated to face outward on the end faces, positioned near the top corners, plus deciding whether to skip them for simplicity.

For materials, I'm planning a wood paint function with noise-based grain and horizontal plank seams, shading faces brighter on top and darker below for a stylized cel look, then applying gilt metal paint for the gold accents like crowns and goblets with a brighter, warmer tone to match the stylized aesthetic.

For the gems, I'm choosing vivid jewel-tone colors and building faceted hexagonal bipyramid shapes via a lathe geometry with six segments and flat shading, then planning to scatter around two dozen of them across the treasure mound and goblets with glow effects.

Now I'm designing the crown: a lathe-generated band with a secondary thin rim, topped with five cone-shaped points, and gems embedded along the front of the band for decoration.

I'm figuring out gem orientation so each cabochon points radially outward from the crown, then working out where to position the crown itself relative to the front goblet pile's center point.

Now I'm checking the pile height at the crown's radius to confirm the band sits flush against the flat-ish top region, and tracing through the coordinate math for placing goblet G1 relative to the main mound's center to get its height right.

I'm computing G2's position similarly, finding it floats about 1.5cm above the surface, and deciding to just lower its y-value to 0.08 to settle it into the coin pile rather than worry about perfect contact.

I'm double-checking G1's placement relative to the chest front, and now verifying the crown's footprint doesn't overlap awkwardly with where G1 sits.

I'm considering whether to add a third goblet lying on its side or on the chest lid, but deciding to skip it and stick with two upright goblets.

I'm planning the goblet's lathe geometry, confirming the axis and segment settings, and thinking about adding a decorative rim band near the bowl using a second smaller lathe ring in a darker gilt tone.

For embellishment, I'm figuring out how to attach a gem to the goblet's bowl surface using a stick primitive oriented with a frame facing outward, positioning it near the bowl's front wall with a small embed depth so it reads as inset into the metal.

I'm scoping the module length to around 550-650 lines given the props group's smaller footprint relative to the full model target. For the painterly LoL-style shading, I'm planning a toon-style lighting function with a directional light vector and a smoothstep-based blend that warms highlights and cools shadows, returning an RGB tuple compatible with the paint API.

Now I'm checking which helpers are actually exported from the SDK — confirming smoothstep, mix, rgb, noise, paint, resolve, svg, frame, and the kit utilities like metal, glow, aim, toDirection, and Spot all come through the top-level package rather than internal paths, so I get the imports right.

Then I'm designing the surface paints: a metal-based gilt finish for the mound using built-in shading, and a wood paint function that computes plank seams via a fractional y-coordinate, blends dark and light wood tones using a noise-driven grain factor, and darkens seam lines with an ink mix before shading by the normal.

I'm checking that plank seams read reasonably on both the lid's arc and chest front, then defining a shading helper that mixes a violet-tinted shadow color with the base color based on a smoothstepped dot product between the normal and light direction, lightening toward a highlight. For metallic parts like the goblet and crown, I'll just rely on the built-in gilt metal paint with tweaked polish rather than custom shading.

For textures I'm sketching coin face SVGs: a gold radial gradient fill with a darker rim ring, outlined stroke, and a simple crown/star emblem shape stamped in a darker brown on top.

I'm settling on three distinct coin/emblem textures total — two gold coin faces with different emblems (crown-style and sun/star) and a shield emblem for the chest lock, drawn as a dark shield outline with a gold border and a red gem accent — keeping silver coins as flat painted color instead of a fourth texture.

For the chest emblem plane, I'm orienting it to face +Z with the drawing upright along +Y. Then I'm adding scattered sparkle cards over the gems and goblets using glowing star textures, generating frames from surface scatter hits so each sparkle sits oriented to the surface it's glinting on.

Writing the sparkle SVG texture...

Now I'm thinking through the import structure, deciding to define a local Rgb type alias rather than relying on a top-level export, and sketching the overall file setup with the builder, paint, and glow kit imports.

I confirm that `glow` applies strength to a target part, and that the metal clockwork kit is compatible with the base builder import path. Painted parts on the lathe mound should bake correctly with the metal paint applied.

Writing the lighting and tone-shading function...

Now I'm defining paint functions for wood, iron, gilt, and brass materials, each using noise-based grain or seam patterns combined with the two-tone shading, followed by gemstone color definitions and the lathe profile geometry for cutting gem shapes.

I'm now generating the lathe-based gem geometry function and sizing variants for small and large gems, then moving to coin geometry using a cylinder shape designed so the circular coin texture maps cleanly onto the flat caps and edge.

I'm checking that `b.stick` supports a texture option alongside its other parameters, then planning coin color variation across gold, silver, and copper tones with occasional textured variants mixed in by index. I'm sketching out a coin-placement function that builds a surface from the mound and front parts to scatter coins across using an array of target Parts.

Now I'm working out the scatter filter logic: excluding hits inside a defined chest region and requiring a minimum upward-facing normal so coins don't land on steep or hidden surfaces, then doing something similar for gems with a tighter minDist and higher normal threshold before sticking them down with an embed depth and flat orientation option.

I'm also placing floating glow effects on gems, then laying out loose floor coins in a ring around the mound center while skipping any that fall too close to the front pile, giving each a small random tilt and spin so they don't look perfectly flat. Tallying up parts (coins, gems, sparks, goblets, chest) to make sure the total count feels right, then scattering a few extra glowing gems directly on the floor near the pile.

Now I'm figuring out how to orient those floor gems so their pointed tip sits at ground level rather than sinking through it, and positioning gems within the goblet bowls using a frame anchored to a point on the bowl's outer surface.

Then I'm sketching out the goblet's lathe profile, working through the outer wall shape up to the rim and the inner wall curving back down into the hollow bowl, checking that the solid stem and base close up correctly without leaving gaps or overlaps.

Now I'm placing the two goblets in the scene with lathe geometry and a gilt color, then adding a scatter of small coin cylinders spilling out from inside one of the goblets to suggest treasure.

Working out the crown shape, I'm sketching its lathe cross-section as a band with a stepped rim profile, trying to combine the band and rim into a single closed polygon outline rather than two overlapping gilt parts.

For the five points of the crown, I'm placing small gilt cones radiating outward at 72-degree intervals around the band, each capped with a tiny glowing gem at its tip, and adding cabochon gems spaced around the front of the band at three symmetric angles.

I'm also working out the chest emblem layout: a gilt lock disc with a textured plane overlaid slightly in front of it, sizing both so the emblem reads clearly without the lock edges peeking out too much.

Then I'm adding side handles made from rotated torus shapes, iron corner brackets as vertical boxes at the chest's edges, and iron bands across the lid positioned at a few x-offsets to simulate reinforced strapping over the wood.

Still defining dimensions: the body as a box spanning the right height range, the lid as a rotated half-cylinder, and two lathe-turned shapes for the central mound and front pile, adjusting their profile points so the tops sit flush with the crown height.

Now I'm checking overlap between the front coin pile and the chest front -- the pile's radius barely grazes the chest base at z=0, so no real clipping there. For coin scattering, I need to add a filter so coins near the crown's footprint don't poke through the crown's base band, since coins placed right at the pile's top surface there would sit just above the band's bottom edge.

I'm filtering out coins too close to the crown center and to the goblet feet, and separately filtering floor coins to avoid the chest's footprint since those floor positions are already far enough from the chest corners to be safe. For the sparkle effect, I'm scattering spark cards onto the pile's upward-facing hit points, excluding ones too low or inside the chest, then applying a glow to the resulting card meshes.

Now I'm also considering whether to glow the crown gems and lock gem. For the skeleton structure, I'm thinking about whether I need to explicitly create a root joint since the model has no joints defined otherwise -- without one, part calls without a bone reference might fail, so I'll create a single root joint and rely on it being the nearest joint to any position, avoiding the need to pass a bone reference on every single part call.

With just one joint existing, I plan to wrap part/lathe calls in a helper that still passes the root bone explicitly for safety, while stick calls will inherit their bone from the surface hit they're placed on. I'm also sequencing the build: mound and front pieces first, then the chest, crown, and goblets, followed by coins and gems scattered across the pile surface (built only from the mound and front, excluding the chest), using separate seeded random generators for variety in placement.

I'm filtering the scatter so coins and gems only land on upward-facing surfaces of the mound, and setting up the module's exported metadata and default build function with minimal, only-necessary imports. I'm also defining a chest-containment check using the hit point's coordinates, and setting up a palette of coin colors with random selection logic for texturing roughly 200 coins across the mound with minimum spacing.

Now I'm working out texture assignment by index for coins, deciding when to apply special textured variants versus plain colored ones, and confirming the stick-building function's signature matches the documented options. I'm sizing the coins, sparks, and card meshes, checking triangle counts stay reasonable, and tallying floor coins mixed with textured variants, while confirming I'm pulling in the right helper functions like smoothstep, mix, noise, rgb, paint, svg, rng, createBuilder, metal, and glow from the SDK and kit.

Setting up imports and chest layout constants...

I'm working through the geometry for the chest footprint so coins don't poke through the chest body—checking which plateau positions fall inside versus outside the chest's bounding box, and making sure the flat mound top near the chest corners gets handled correctly.

Now I'm setting up the lathe shapes for the mound, front pile, and goblets, using a surface builder that accepts nested arrays of shapes for the coin pile placement. Then I'm building the crown function, which creates a lathe ring and five small cones arranged radially around it at an angle offset, positioning each cone's center height relative to the crown's base point.

I'm placing tiny gems on the cone tips and small cabochon gems around the crown band at three angles, orienting each gem's direction outward with the band's y-axis default, then adding a glow effect to crown gems since they use flat (non-painted) materials compatible with the glow function. Finally I'm positioning larger gems on the goblet bowls, calculating the protrusion offset so they sit just outside the bowl's curved surface facing outward in the z-direction.

Now I'm shifting to the chest construction: building a half-cylinder lid with wood paint, adding three iron bands across it rotated to match the lid's orientation, then constructing the box-shaped body beneath it and adding vertical iron straps down the front face at three x-positions.

I'm positioning a cylindrical iron lock disc centered on the front face, aligning it so it doesn't clash with the middle strap, then adding a small emblem plane just in front of it. I'm also considering whether to add horizontal iron bands or skip them, and placing decorative gilt corner posts at the four body corners, checking that they don't overlap the front straps.

Now I'm adding ring-shaped handles on each side using torus geometry rotated to lie flat against the side faces, positioned slightly outward from the box edges. I'm also planning the SVG textures for sparkle effects and coin details that will scatter near the chest.

Designing coin SVG textures...

Finishing the lighting helper with low/high shading blended by light dot product, then defining the wood paint with plank seams, grain noise, and ink darkening, feeding it through the toning function. Now I'm setting up gilt and brass metal paints with tarnish parameters for the remaining materials.

Writing coin color palette and scatter setup...

Setting up the builder scaffold with named joints and seeded RNGs for positioning, confirming that rng(seed) returns a callable usable directly in scatter and tileBox options.

Writing coin placement scatter logic with distance filters to avoid the chest, crown, and goblets...

Scattering coins loosely across the floor around the pile, skipping any that land too close to the player, with randomized rotation for a natural scattered look.

I'm also placing a few upright gems on the floor beyond the mound's edge, working out their sizing and vertical offset so the pointed tip of each gem profile sits flush with the ground.

I'm deciding whether to add a gem to the lock's emblem but choosing to skip it since the ruby already covers that spot. Now I'm writing helper functions that check whether a point falls within the chest's body bounds or near the crown, to help place hit effects correctly.

Then I'm defining the goblet positions and lathe outline arrays for the mound shape, making sure each outline forms a proper closed solid that starts and ends on the axis — verifying the mound profile closes correctly without leaving gaps.

Working through more outline arrays for the pile, crown ring with its band geometry, and the gem profile, which gets built as a hexagonal lathe geometry via THREE.LatheGeometry with six phi segments. I'm settling on using a stick helper with flat shading for the gem, and sketching a factory function that maps the gem profile points into scaled Vector2s for the lathe. Writing more lathe build code...

Now I'm placing coins inside the goblet's interior at specific relative heights above the goblet's base position, checking that the cup's inner floor and rim measurements line up so the coins sit correctly within the bowl without clipping the walls. I'm also verifying the crown's cabochon placement height and sketching a glow effect wrapped around card sprites, then double-checking the signature for the cards helper and starting to build a surface call involving a mound shape.

I'm thinking about adding more decorative richness to the chest -- gilded rivet studs placed in rows along the iron straps and lid bands, using small spheres at specific coordinates to suggest hardware detail, aiming to flesh out the module to a fuller length appropriate for a finished prop group.

I'm also considering extra pile elements: a thin gilt lathe ring at the goblet's rim, a tipped-over second goblet or scattered coins, and a velvet drawstring pouch sitting against the coin pile, working out its lathe profile coordinates and a gold neck ring to add color contrast and material variety to the scene.

Now I'm positioning the pouch on the pile and checking its distance from the goblets to avoid overlap, then setting up a shared blocker system so coins, gems, and sparkles get filtered out near the crown, goblets, and pouch using radius checks, plus defining the velvet paint material for the pouch's toned color.

Writing scene setup code...

I'm placing the pile mound at its center, then checking that the lid's half-cylinder geometry sits correctly with its flat edge at TOP_Y and the arc spanning upward, with end caps forming proper half-discs.

Still defining more parts: adding the emblem texture plane, confirming the joint position type, and setting up gem colors cycling through ruby, sapphire, and emerald for the crown cabochons. I'm now writing helper functions to check if a point is blocked by obstacles or falls within the chest's bounding box, though I notice the chest bounds calculation might be inflating the region slightly more than intended.

I'm reconsidering whether to add a typed helper function for placing parts, but decide it's simpler to skip it and rely on the default behavior where each mesh attaches to its nearest joint—since there's only one root joint, everything naturally binds there without needing an explicit bone reference.

I confirm I do need to create the root joint, since calling b.part without any joints present could fail. Now I'm writing a shading helper function that blends a base color toward a shadow tone and a highlight tone based on the surface normal's alignment with a light direction, producing a toned color for lighting parts of the mesh.

Defining gold, velvet, and pile paint materials for the coins and cloth, then setting up the coin geometry as a short cylinder and adding a glow effect around the gem shapes before assembling everything into the final scene root.

I decide to skip assigning the joint to a variable to avoid an unused-variable lint issue, calling `b.joint` directly without capturing its result. Then I move on to drafting the coin SVG texture and chest geometry, including the iron lid material and lid cylinder shape.

Adding straps, studs, lock, and emblem details...

Finalizing the ruby placement and double-checking the stroke width scales correctly against the viewBox, then assembling the complete module.
